Notes on keeping bees in a city flat

What two summers on a fifth-floor balcony taught me

When I told my neighbours I was going to keep bees on the balcony, most of them assumed I was joking. Two summers later the hive has produced eleven jars of honey and exactly one complaint, which was about the noise of the extractor rather than the bees themselves.

Choosing the hive

A balcony hive has to be light enough to carry up the stairs in pieces and narrow enough to leave room for a person to work beside it. I settled on a top-bar design, which needs no heavy supers and lets you inspect one comb at a time without lifting the whole box.

Water and neighbours

Bees need water close to the hive, or they will find it in the nearest dripping air conditioner. A shallow tray with pebbles keeps them at home and away from the neighbours' plant saucers, which matters more for good relations than any amount of free honey.

I also learned to inspect the hive early in the morning, when most of the foragers are still inside and the building is quiet. An inspection at lunchtime once sent a cloud of curious bees past the window of the flat downstairs.

The first harvest

The first harvest came in late August. City honey is dark and surprisingly floral, thanks to the lime trees along the canal and the window boxes that nobody thinks of as forage.
